faqs.a: d stands for die, and the number is the side count. d6 is the classic cube, d20 is the 20-sided die of role-playing games, and d100 gives a 1 to 100 percentile roll. Pick the die your game asks for.
faqs.q: What does d6 or d20 mean?

faqs.a: Every face has the same 1-in-n chance. There is no memory and no pattern. Over many rolls each number appears about equally often, which is exactly what a fair physical die does.

For 2d6 there are 36 equally likely pairs. Six of them total 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1). So P(7) = 6/36 = 1/6, about 16.7 percent. Only (6,6) totals 12, so P(12) = 1/36, about 2.8 percent.
faqs.q: Why is 7 the most common total on 2d6?

faqs.a: The expected value of one die is (1 + n) / 2. For a d20 that is 10.5, for 3d6 it is 3 x 3.5 = 10.5. The tool shows the expected total under every roll.
For casual games with friends, yes. For tournaments or money games, use physical dice everyone can see. A screen result cannot be verified by the other players.
faqs.q: Can I use this for a real game night?

faqs.a: The d100 (percentile die) covers that: it returns 1 to 100 uniformly. Two d10 dice, one for tens and one for units, is the classic physical method; a single d100 does the same job here.
faqs.q: How do I roll a percentage (1-100)?

keyFacts: A fair n-sided die lands on each face with probability 1/n.
The classic d6 has expected value 3.5. Every die's average is (1 + n) / 2.
Two dice do not give a flat distribution: on 2d6, 7 is six times more likely than 2 or 12.
The d20 is the signature die of tabletop role-playing games like Dungeons and Dragons.
A d100 roll is called a percentile roll and is used for percentage chances.

dice-roller.workedExample:
Rolling 2d6:
1. Range: 2 to 12. Expected total: 2 x 3.5 = 7.
2. You roll 4 and 5: total 9.
3. How likely was that? Pairs totalling 9: (3,6), (4,5), (5,4), (6,3) = 4 out of 36, so P(9) = 4/36 = 1/9, about 11.1 percent.
4. Compare: P(7) = 6/36 = 1/6 (16.7%), P(12) = 1/36 (2.8%). Middle totals are always more likely than extremes.
